opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's a pleasure to be here.

This is one of the most exciting shifts I've seen in my career. For decades, the hardest problem in robotics wasn't the hardware or even the control. It was common sense. A robot could weld a car door with sub-millimeter precision, but it had no idea that a cup of water tips over if you hold it sideways, or that you shouldn't put a knife on the edge of a table where a child can reach it. We tried to hand-code that knowledge, rule by rule, and it never scaled. The world is simply too long-tailed.

Foundation models change that in a fundamental way. When you train a large model on internet-scale text, images, and video, it absorbs an enormous amount of implicit knowledge about how the world works: what objects are for, how people behave, what usually follows what. So instead of programming common sense, the robot can inherit it. You can tell a robot "clean up the kitchen," and the model already has a reasonable prior that dishes go in the sink, food goes in the fridge, and trash goes in the bin.

But I want to be careful here. Language and vision models give you semantic common sense, the "what" and the "why." They don't automatically give you physical common sense, the "how": how much force to apply, how a soft object deforms, how friction behaves on a wet surface. That kind of knowledge comes from interaction, from embodiment. So I think the real frontier now is combining the two, connecting the broad knowledge of foundation models with physical data from robots acting in the world, through vision-language-action models, simulation, world models, and large-scale real-world data collection.

In my view, we're moving from information intelligence to physical intelligence, and eventually to biological intelligence. Foundation models are the bridge. They give robots a head start on understanding the world, but the robot still has to learn to live in it. And that's where a lot of the hard and interesting work will happen over the next several years: data, safety, and making sure these systems remain reliable and aligned with human values as they leave the screen and enter our homes, roads, and factories.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is actually one of the most profound shifts we've seen in robotics in the past twenty years. Let me explain why.

For a very long time, the bottleneck in robotics was not the hardware. We had decent motors, decent sensors, decent control systems. The bottleneck was intelligence, and specifically common sense. A robot could be programmed to pick up a cup in a laboratory, but if you moved the cup ten centimeters, or changed the lighting, or replaced the cup with a mug, the whole thing would break. The robot had no understanding of what a cup is, what it is for, or what happens when you tip it over.

Humans acquire this kind of knowledge through years of embodied experience, and also through language, through culture, through what other people tell us. Robots had neither. Every robot had to learn everything from scratch, in its own narrow environment, with its own narrow data.

What foundation models change is that, for the first time, robots can inherit a large amount of world knowledge that was learned elsewhere. A large language model or a vision-language model has read essentially everything humans have written and seen a very large fraction of what humans have photographed. So it already knows that glass breaks, that liquids spill, that you should not put a wet towel on a laptop, that a kitchen usually has a sink near the stove. This is exactly the common sense that was missing. You no longer have to teach each robot these things one by one.

Now, I want to be careful here, because there are two different layers. The first is semantic common sense, understanding what objects are and how the world generally works. Foundation models are very good at this. The second is physical common sense, understanding how much force to apply, how an object will move when you push it, how to keep balance. This is still much harder, because the Internet does not contain enough of this kind of data. You cannot learn how it feels to hold an egg by reading about eggs.

So what we are seeing now, and what I find very exciting, is the convergence of these two. People are building what we call vision-language-action models, where the same large model that understands language and images also outputs motor commands. And the data for the physical part is coming from simulation, from teleoperation, from large fleets of robots collecting experience together. In some sense, the foundation model provides the brain, the prior, the general understanding, and then embodied data grounds that understanding in the physical world.

I often say that the previous wave of AI was about the digital world, and this wave is about the physical world. Autonomous driving was actually the first large-scale embodied AI application, and we learned a lot from it, including how important scale and data flywheels are. Humanoid robots and general-purpose robots are the next step.

If I had to summarize, I would say foundation models turn the robot's common sense problem from a cold start problem into a fine-tuning problem. That is an enormous change. It does not solve everything, and I think we are still several years away from a truly general household robot. But the trajectory is now clear, and the pace is much faster than I expected even three years ago.

r001.rationale: The response calls autonomous driving an early embodied AI application and humanoid robots the next step, but does not contrast driving’s narrower scope with the variety of everyday robot tasks.

r002.rationale: The response discusses robots failing when a cup changes or is replaced by a mug, but does not say they can generalize an opening skill to unfamiliar objects.

r003.rationale: It says robots can inherit common sense from foundation models and that each robot no longer has to be taught these things one by one.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe a robot using knowledge of a person’s preferences to infer an appropriate action.

astra-6.text:
I think foundation models change the starting point for robotics. Traditionally, we had to build a robot for a very specific task and give it very specific rules. But the real world has too many situations for us to describe every possibility.

A foundation model can provide a broad base of knowledge about objects, language, and relationships. If you ask a robot to bring you a glass of water, it can help connect that instruction to a sequence of actions. The challenge is that knowing what a glass is and knowing how to pick it up without breaking it are different things.

So the robot still needs to learn through perception, action, and feedback. It needs to connect that general knowledge to the physical world—to weight, friction, distance, and the consequences of its movements. Foundation models give us a powerful starting point, but common sense for a robot has to include knowing what it can do safely, and when it needs to stop and ask for help.

sol-6.1.text:
I think foundation models give robotics a very important starting point. Traditionally, we had to teach a robot each task quite explicitly. With foundation models, the robot can draw on knowledge learned from language, images, and video. It can connect an instruction like “clean the table” with objects, actions, and some understanding of what the person intends.

But knowing about the world is different from acting in it. A model may know that a glass is fragile, but a robot still has to learn how much force to apply, how to grasp it, and what to do if it slips. That requires interaction with the physical world and feedback.

So I see foundation models providing broad prior knowledge, while embodied learning grounds that knowledge in experience. The exciting possibility is that robots can then generalize to new situations with much less task-specific training. The challenge is making that common sense reliable enough for real-world action.

r002.rationale: It mentions generalizing to new situations, but does not state that a robot can apply an opening skill to unfamiliar objects.

r003.rationale: It says foundation models provide broad prior knowledge and let robots generalize with much less task-specific training, after contrasting this with explicitly teaching each task.
